'''''Lunaria annua''''', commonly called '''honesty''' or '''annual honesty''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the cabbage and mustard family [[Brassicaceae]]. It is [[native plant|native]] to southern Europe, and cultivated throughout the [[temperate climate|temperate]] world.
[[Image:LunariaAnnua1.jpg|thumb|Ripe pods ([[silique]]s), some with seeds visible, some with only the central membrane remaining]]

==Description==
It is an [[annual plant|annual]] or [[biennial plant|biennial]] growing to {{convert|90|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall by {{convert|30|cm|0|abbr=on}} broad, with large, coarse, pointed oval leaves with marked serrations. The leaves are hairy, the lower ones long-stalked, the upper ones stalkless.<ref name="Parnell">Parnell, J. and Curtis, T. 2012 ''Webb's An Irish Flora.'' Cork University Press {{ISBN|978-185918-4783}}</ref> In spring and summer it bears terminal [[raceme]]s of white, pink or violet flowers, followed by a kind of showy, green-through-light-brown, translucent, disc-shaped<ref name="Parnell"/> [[silique]] called a sillicle (not true botanical seedpods), sometimes called moonpennies.<ref>{{Cite web |date=22 April 2023 |title=Honesty (Lunaria annua) plants for cottage garden |url=https://plantwild.co.uk/product/honesty/ |website=Plant Wild}}</ref>  When a silique is ripe and dry, a valve on each of its sides readily falls off, and its seeds fall off a central membrane which has a silvery sheen, {{convert|3|-|8|cm|0|abbr=on}} in diameter; the membrane can persist on a plant throughout a winter depending on the weather.<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1405332965|pages=1136}}</ref> These sillicles are much used in dry [[Flower arranging|floral arrangements]].

==Distribution==
''Lunaria annua'' is native to southern Europe from Spain to Romania, and has been introduced to many other parts of the world with temperate climates.<ref name=powo/>

==Names==
The Latin name ''lunaria'' means 'moon-shaped' and refers to the shape and appearance of this species' [[silique]]s.<ref name=AZPLA>{{cite book|last=Coombes|first=Allen J.|title=The A to Z of plant names|year=2012|publisher=Timber Press|location=USA|isbn=9781604691962|pages=[https://archive.org/details/isbn_9781604691962/page/312 312]|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9781604691962/page/312}}</ref> The common name "honesty" arose in the 16th century<ref>{{Cite web |title=Oxford University Plants 400: Lunaria annua |url=https://herbaria.plants.ox.ac.uk/bol/plants400/Profiles/KL/Lunaria#:~:text=It%20is%20known%20as%20Honesty,Elizabethan%20musical%20manuscripts,%20called%20pricksongs.&text=Leins%20P%20et%20al.,anemochory%20of%20Lunaria%20(Brassicaceae). |access-date=2024-05-10 |website=herbaria.plants.ox.ac.uk}}</ref> and relates to the translucence of its silique membranes, which "truthfully" reveal their contents. Additional English names include ''money plant'', ''moneywort'', ''penny flower'', ''silver dollar'', and ''money-in-both-pockets'',<ref name="OxfordPlans400">{{cite web |last1=Todd |first1=Jamie |title=Plant 235 - Lunaria annua L. (Brassicaceae) - Honesty |url=https://herbaria.plants.ox.ac.uk/bol/plants400/Profiles/kl/Lunaria |website=Plants 400 |publisher=Department of Plant Sciences, University of Oxford |access-date=5 March 2022 |quote=There are plenty of common names, many referring to money such as money plant, moneywort, penny flower, silver dollar and money-in-both-pockets.}}</ref> ''Chinese money'', or ''Chinese coins''. These, too, reference the silique membranes, which have the appearance of silvery coins. In French, it is known as {{Lang|fr|monnaie du pape}} ("Pope's money").  In Denmark it is known as {{Lang|da|judaspenge}} and in Dutch-speaking countries as {{Lang|nl|judaspenning}} (both meaning "coins of Judas"), an allusion to the story of [[Judas Iscariot]] and the [[thirty pieces of silver]] he was paid for betraying Christ.<ref>"Judaspenning", ''[[Van Dale]]'s Groot woordenboek van de Nederlandse taal'', online edition, retrieved 23 May 2020</ref>

==Symbolism==
According to the Victorian era [[language of flowers]] published by American [[Sarah Josepha Hale]], the plant represents fascination or sentiment.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Hale |first1=Sarah Josepha Buell |author-link1=Sarah Josepha Hale |date=1856 |title=Flora's Interpreter, and Fortuna Flora |url=https://archive.org/details/florasinterprete00haleiala |edition=Revised and enlarged |location=Boston, Massachusetts |publisher=Sanborn, Carter and Bazin |page=87 |oclc=498324 |access-date=25 June 2026}}</ref> In other systems its meanings include honesty and money.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gips |first1=Kathleen M. |date=1990 |title=The Language of Flowers |url=https://archive.org/details/bwb_Y0-DSM-165 |edition=Revised and enlarged |location=Chagrin Falls, Ohio |publisher=Pine Creek Press |page=83 |oclc=682012825 |access-date=25 June 2026}}</ref> In witchcraft, the honesty plant is considered protective, being thought to keep away monsters, evil spirits, and demons.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Lehner |first1=Ernst |last2=Lehner |first2=Johanna |date=1960 |title=Folklore and Symbolism of Flowers, Plants, and Trees |url=https://archive.org/details/folkloresymbolis0000unse |url-access=registration |location=New York |publisher=Tudor Pub. Co |page=88 |oclc=498324 |access-date=25 June 2026}}</ref> The plant is also used in spells for prosperity, the flat pods (when ripe and silvery) resembling coins and therefore being seen as symbolising promises of wealth. In the earliest surviving recipe for a [[flying ointment]] (recorded by [[Bavaria]]n physician [[Johannes Hartlieb]] circa 1440), ''Lunaria'' is included as the herbal ingredient corresponding [[Astrology|astrologically]] to the moon and therefore to be picked on the lunar day of Monday.<ref>Hartlieb, Johannes, ''das puch aller verpoten kunst, ungelaubens und der zaubrey'', 1450s, [http://digi.ub.uni-heidelberg.de/cpg478 CPG 478], 78 foll. (in the hand of [[Clara Hätzlerin]]), 1465, ed. Eisermann and Graf (1989).</ref>

==Cultivation==
This plant is easy to grow from seed and tends to naturalize. It is usually grown as a biennial, being sown one year to flower the next. It is suitable for cultivation in a shady or dappled area, or in a wildflower garden, and the flowers and dried siliques are often seen in [[flower arrangements]].<ref name=AZPLA /> Numerous [[variety (botany)|varieties]] and [[cultivar]]s are available, of which the white-flowered ''L. annua'' var. ''albiflora''<ref>{{cite web|title=Lunaria annua var. albiflora, white-flowered honesty | url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/89962/lunaria-annua-var-albiflora/details | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 8 May 2023}}</ref> and the [[variegation|variegated]] white ''L. annua'' var. ''albiflora'' 'Alba Variegata'<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/83138/lunaria-annua-var-albiflora-alba-variegata-(v)/details | title =Lunaria annua var. albiflora 'Alba Variegata&' (v), honesty 'Alba Variegata' | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 8 May 2023}}</ref> have won the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 
| page = 62 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 25 March 2018}}</ref>
